In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel error detection system for clinical intracortically recorded brain–computer interfaces (iBCIs) that will enable the automatic correction of errors in the user’s movement intention.
the development of a novel approach to improve the performance and usability of intracortical brain-computer interface (BCI) systems.
developing a new generation of BCIs that will be more accurate, more robust, and less frustrating for the user.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the neural activity of human motor cortex is rich with information that can potentially improve BCI performance, including the ability of the system to detect errors and automatically intervene with a corrective action.

the neural activity recorded from the human motor cortex contains a putative error signal that can be decoded with very high accuracy and can be utilized as the basis of a real-time automatic error detect-and-unde system for BCI control.

the results of our study suggest that the error signal in human motor cortical spiking and field potentials is sufficiently robust to be utilized for the development of a real-time error-detect-and-undo system for clinical intracortically-recorded BCIs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human motor cortex is a rich source of signals that can be used for a variety of applications, including the automatic detection and correction of errors.
we can decode the outcome of a movement intention from the intracortically recorded neural activity in the human hand cortex.
we have identified neural correlates of task outcome error in the human motor cortex and have shown that it is possible to detect and correct these errors in real time.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the neural activity of the hand area of motor cortical cortex reflects the outcome of movement attempts and can be decoded with sufficient accuracy for a system to detect errors and intervene with corrective actions.
there are neural correlates of task outcomes in the human motor cortex and these correlates can be used to detect and undo errors in a real-time BCI system.
there is a putative neural correlate to error detection in motor cortex, and it is possible to detect errors with a very high level of accuracy.
